mainTopic: Interrupting קריאת שמע and הלל to greet someone, tasting on a fast day, greeting and personal business before תפלה, and the ruling on not pausing between אלהיכם and אמת ויציב
overview: The amud opens by finishing the גמרא's corrected reading of the משנה about greeting people during קריאת שמע, and a ברייתא confirms that wording. Next, רבי חייא rules that one may interrupt הלל and מגילה to greet someone. רבה then adds a limit: on days of complete הלל, one may stop only between paragraphs. A story about רבינא seems to contradict רבה, but the גמרא explains it away. Then רבי אמי rules that a person who is fasting may taste food, up to a רביעית. רב teaches that greeting someone before תפלה is like building a במה. רבי אבא limits this to going early to a person's door on purpose. The גמרא adds that doing your own business before praying is forbidden, and that praying before a journey brings blessing. After a side discussion on a פסוק about sleep and dreams, רבי יוחנן rules like רבי יהודה that one may not pause between אלהיכם and אמת ויציב. The source for that ruling begins on the next amud.

steps.title: End of the corrected wording of the משנה: רבי יהודה on the breaks between paragraphs
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes its corrected reading of רבי יהודה's view. Between the paragraphs of שמע, a person may start a greeting out of respect and may answer anyone's greeting.
steps.simpleTranslation: And at the breaks between the paragraphs, he may greet out of respect and answer 'shalom' to any person.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a sentence it began earlier. It is supplying missing words in the משנה so that רבי יהודה's view makes sense.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before this, the משנה looked difficult because the wording seemed incomplete. The גמרא solves this by saying words are missing (חסורי מחסרא). With those words added, רבי יהודה says that between paragraphs you may start a greeting out of respect, and you may answer any person at all. Once the wording is filled in, the earlier difficulty disappears.

keyTerms.meaning: The breaks between the paragraphs of שמע
Starts a greeting (literally 'asks' about someone's welfare)
Answers a greeting that someone else started
Out of respect (for example, for a teacher or an important person)

steps.confusionAlert: This line is not a new statement. It is the last piece of the גמרא's corrected version of the משנה, which began on the previous amud.

phrases.english: And at the breaks between the paragraphs —
he may greet out of respect
and he may answer 'shalom' to any person.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּבַפְּרָקִים שׁוֹאֵל מִפְּנֵי הַכָּבוֹד וּמֵשִׁיב שָׁלוֹם לְכׇל אָדָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the corrected wording of the משנה that began on the previous amud.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Textual emendation (חסורי מחסרא): adding words that are missing from the משנה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה's wording seemed incomplete or contradictory about what רבי יהודה allows.
steps.terutzMaskana: According to רבי יהודה, between paragraphs one may start a greeting out of respect and may answer anyone.

steps.title: A ברייתא that matches the corrected wording
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא records the disagreement between רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה in exactly the wording the גמרא just proposed. This supports the correction.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was also taught this way: One who is reading שמע and meets his teacher or someone greater than him may do the following. Between paragraphs, he may greet out of respect, and it goes without saying that he may answer. In the middle of a paragraph, he may greet out of fear, and it goes without saying that he may answer. This is רבי מאיר's view. רבי יהודה says: In the middle, he may greet out of fear and answer out of respect. Between paragraphs, he may greet out of respect and answer anyone.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to show that its corrected reading of the משנה is not invented. A ברייתא actually teaches it this way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר's rule is: whatever you may start, you may certainly answer. In the middle you may start out of fear, and between paragraphs you may start out of respect. רבי יהודה is more lenient about answering. In the middle you may even answer out of respect. Between paragraphs you may answer any person. Because the ברייתא matches the proposed wording word for word, the correction is supported.

keyTerms.meaning: It was also taught this way: a ברייתא supports what was just said
The middle of a paragraph
Out of fear (of someone who could harm you, such as a dangerous person or a king)
It goes without saying

steps.confusionAlert: Fear is the stronger reason, and respect is the weaker one. That is why the middle of a paragraph, which is the stricter place, requires fear before you may start a greeting.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the basic levels: middle of a paragraph versus between paragraphs, and fear versus respect. The rest of the discussion, including the question about הלל, builds on these levels.

phrases.english: It was also taught this way (in a baraita):
One who is reading Shema

phrases.aramaic: וּפָגַע בּוֹ רַבּוֹ אוֹ גָּדוֹל הֵימֶנּוּ,
phrases.english: and his teacher, or someone greater than him, meets him,
between the paragraphs — he may greet out of respect
and it goes without saying that he may answer;
and in the middle — he may greet out of fear
and it goes without saying that he may answer.
These are the words of Rabbi Meir.
Rabbi Yehuda says:
In the middle — he may greet out of fear
and he may answer out of respect;
and between the paragraphs — he may greet out of respect
and he may answer 'shalom' to any person.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the corrected wording from Step 1 with a ברייתא that says the same thing.
steps.raayaObject: The corrected wording of the משנה, including the disagreement between רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that records the disagreement in exactly this wording
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The corrected reading of the משנה is confirmed by a ברייתא.

steps.title: May one interrupt הלל and the מגילה?
steps.stepSummary: אחי asks רבי חייא whether one may stop in the middle of הלל or מגילה to greet someone. He offers two possible ways to think about it.
steps.simpleTranslation: אחי, the תנא of רבי חייא's study hall, asked רבי חייא: May one interrupt during הלל or the מגילה? Do we say there is a קל וחומר: if one may interrupt קריאת שמע, which is from the Torah, then surely one may interrupt הלל, which is only rabbinic? Or perhaps publicizing the miracle is more important?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question. We have learned that one may interrupt שמע, so what about הלל and מגילה?
steps.deeperAnalysis: One side uses a קל וחומר. שמע is a Torah obligation and may be interrupted, so הלל, which is only rabbinic, should be even easier to interrupt. The other side says הלל and מגילה have a special purpose, which is to publicize a miracle (פרסומי ניסא). That purpose might make them stricter than שמע, even though they are only rabbinic.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked him (a real question)
Here: a person whose job was to memorize and recite ברייתות in the study hall
A logical argument from the lighter case to the stricter case
From the Torah / from the Rabbis
Publicizing the miracle

steps.confusionAlert: Here מבעיא?! means 'is there even a question?' It is the second half of the קל וחומר argument. It is not a separate question.

phrases.english: Aḥai asked
(the tanna of the study hall of Rabbi Ḥiyya)
of Rabbi Ḥiyya:
During Hallel and the Megillah,
what is the law: may he interrupt?
Do we say a kal vachomer:
Shema, which is from the Torah — he may interrupt;
Hallel, which is rabbinic — is there even a question?!
Or perhaps
publicizing the miracle is more important.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ אַחַי תַּנָּא דְבֵי רַבִּי חִיָּיא מֵרַבִּי חִיָּיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the rule about interrupting שמע and asks whether it extends to הלל and מגילה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether one may interrupt הלל and מגילה to greet someone, given that they are rabbinic but are meant to publicize a miracle.

steps.title: רבי חייא: one may interrupt
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא answers that one may interrupt הלל and מגילה, and that this is no problem.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: He may interrupt, and there is nothing wrong with it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חייא answers אחי's question. Interrupting is permitted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי חייא accepts the קל וחומר. Publicizing the miracle does not make הלל stricter than שמע. The phrase 'there is nothing wrong with it' means the interruption causes no loss of the מצוה.

keyTerms.meaning: He interrupts or stops
There is nothing wrong with it

phrases.english: He (Rabbi Ḥiyya) said to him:
He may interrupt, and there is nothing wrong with it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ פּוֹסֵק וְאֵין בְּכָךְ כְּלוּם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question asked in Step 3.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: One may interrupt הלל and מגילה. The קל וחומר from שמע holds.

steps.title: רבה: it depends on whether הלל is complete on that day
steps.stepSummary: רבה adds a distinction. On days when complete הלל is said, one may interrupt only between paragraphs. On days when it is not complete, one may interrupt even in the middle of a paragraph.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: On days when an individual completes the הלל, he may interrupt between one paragraph and the next, but not in the middle of a paragraph. On days when an individual does not complete the הלל, he may interrupt even in the middle of a paragraph.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה refines רבי חייא's answer by explaining exactly when and where one may stop during הלל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Days of complete הלל, such as the holidays, are a real rabbinic obligation. On those days, one may stop only between paragraphs, similar to the breaks in שמע. Days of partial הלל, such as ראש חודש, are only a custom. On those days, one may stop even in the middle of a paragraph. The stronger the obligation, the more limited the interruption.

keyTerms.meaning: Says the complete הלל
An individual (praying alone)
Between one paragraph and the next

steps.whatToRemember: Interrupting הלל: on days of complete הלל (an obligation), only between paragraphs. On days of partial הלל (a custom), even in the middle of a paragraph.
steps.confusionAlert: 'Days when the individual does not complete' does not mean days with no הלל at all. It means days when the shortened (partial) הלל is said only as a custom.
steps.whyThisMatters: This becomes the practical rule for interrupting הלל, and it ties the strictness of interrupting to how strong the obligation is.

phrases.english: Rabbah said:

phrases.aramaic: יָמִים שֶׁהַיָּחִיד גּוֹמֵר בָּהֶן אֶת הַהַלֵּל,
phrases.english: Days on which the individual completes the Hallel —
between one paragraph and the next he may interrupt;
in the middle of the paragraph — he may not interrupt.

phrases.aramaic: וְיָמִים שֶׁאֵין הַיָּחִיד גּוֹמֵר בָּהֶן אֶת הַהַלֵּל —
phrases.english: And days on which the individual does not complete the Hallel —
even in the middle of the paragraph he may interrupt.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה יָמִים שֶׁהַיָּחִיד גּוֹמֵר בָּהֶן אֶת הַהַלֵּל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits רבי חייא's general permission by distinguishing between kinds of days and places within הלל.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Complete-הלל days: interrupt only between paragraphs. Partial-הלל days: interrupt even in the middle of a paragraph.

steps.title: A story where רבינא did not stop his הלל to greet someone
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבה's rule. On a day when הלל is not complete, רבינא did not stop to greet רב בר שבא, even though רבה said one may interrupt even in the middle of a paragraph.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that really so? רב בר שבא once came to רבינא on a day when an individual does not say the complete הלל, and רבינא did not stop to greet him!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions רבה's rule by bringing a story about רבינא. If interrupting was allowed on that day, why didn't רבינא stop to greet his visitor?
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה said that on days of partial הלל you may interrupt even in the middle of a paragraph. Here, on exactly such a day, רבינא did not interrupt for רב בר שבא. That behavior seems to show that interrupting is not allowed, which contradicts רבה.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that so?! The opening of a challenge
But look, here is a case where...
Happened to come, arrived
Interrupted, stopped

phrases.english: Is that so?! But Rav bar Shaba
phrases.notes: The opening of the challenge against רבה.

phrases.english: happened to come to Ravina,

phrases.aramaic: וְיָמִים שֶׁאֵין הַיָּחִיד גּוֹמֵר אֶת הַהַלֵּל הֲוָה,
phrases.english: and it was one of the days when an individual does not complete the Hallel,
phrases.notes: These are the exact days on which רבה allowed interrupting even mid-paragraph.

phrases.english: and he did not interrupt for him!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִינִי?! וְהָא רַב בַּר שְׁבָא אִיקְּלַע לְגַבֵּיהּ דְּרָבִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבה's rule from Step 5 using a real-life story
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's rule that on days of partial הלל one may interrupt even in the middle of a paragraph
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבינא, on a day of partial הלל, did not interrupt to greet רב בר שבא. This suggests interrupting is not permitted.

steps.title: רבינא did not consider רב בר שבא important enough to stop for
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the story proves nothing about the rule. רבינא did not stop only because רב בר שבא was not someone he felt he needed to honor in the middle of הלל.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב בר שבא is different, because he was not considered important in רבינא's eyes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. Stopping was allowed, but רבינא chose not to stop because he did not see רב בר שבא as important enough.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Permission to interrupt is not an obligation to interrupt. The היתר is there out of respect for an important person. Since רבינא did not view רב בר שבא that way, there was no reason to stop, so רבה's rule stands.

keyTerms.meaning: It is different. Used to say a case does not fit the general rule
Important, considered significant

steps.whatToRemember: On days of partial הלל, one may interrupt even mid-paragraph to greet someone. The story of רבינא does not disprove this, because he was simply not obligated to stop for someone he did not consider important.

phrases.english: Rav bar Shaba is different,
since he was not considered important in Ravina's eyes.
phrases.notes: So there was no need to interrupt for him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 6 and protects רבה's rule
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the case: the story involved a person who did not warrant interruption
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבינא's silence shows that interrupting is forbidden on days of partial הלל
steps.terutzMaskana: Interrupting is permitted, but only someone worth honoring calls for it. רב בר שבא was not that important to רבינא.

steps.title: May a person who is fasting taste food?
steps.stepSummary: אשיאן, the תנא of רבי אמי's study hall, asks רבי אמי whether someone fasting may taste food. He gives two sides: maybe the fast forbids only eating and drinking, or maybe it forbids any enjoyment of food.
steps.simpleTranslation: אשיאן, the תנא of the school of רבי אמי, asked רבי אמי: May someone who is fasting taste food? Did he accept upon himself not to eat and drink, and tasting is not eating and drinking? Or perhaps he accepted upon himself not to have pleasure from food, and tasting does give pleasure?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now moves to a new question, again asked by a תנא, just like the question of אחי earlier. The question is whether tasting food breaks a fast.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everything depends on what the person took on when he started the fast. If he took on 'no eating and drinking,' tasting is not real eating, so it is allowed. If he took on 'no enjoyment from food,' tasting still gives some enjoyment, so it would be forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked him, he raised a question before him
Here: a person in the study hall who memorized and recited ברייתות and משניות
One who is in the middle of a fast
He accepted upon himself
Pleasure, enjoyment
Or perhaps. Introduces the second side of a question

phrases.english: Ashyan asked

phrases.aramaic: תַּנָּא דְבֵי רַבִּי אַמֵּי מֵרַבִּי אַמֵּי:
phrases.english: the tanna of the school of Rabbi Ami, of Rabbi Ami:
One who is fasting, may he taste?
phrases.notes: For example, tasting a dish to check whether it is spiced properly.

phrases.english: Did he accept upon himself not to eat and drink?
phrases.notes: First side of the question.

phrases.english: And this is not eating and drinking.
Or perhaps he accepted upon himself not to have pleasure?
phrases.notes: Second side of the question.

phrases.english: And this is pleasure.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ אַשְׁיָאן תַּנָּא דְבֵי רַבִּי אַמֵּי מֵרַבִּי אַמֵּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic. It is linked to the earlier question (Step 3) because both were asked by a תנא of the study hall.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does tasting food count as breaking a fast? Is the fast defined by eating and drinking, or by enjoyment?

steps.title: רבי אמי: tasting is fine
steps.stepSummary: רבי אמי answers that a person who is fasting may taste, and it is no problem.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: He tastes, and there is nothing wrong with it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אמי answers the question. A fasting person may taste food.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer follows the first side of the question. The fast is about eating and drinking, and tasting is not considered eating.

keyTerms.meaning: He tastes
There is nothing to it, it is no problem

steps.confusionAlert: Tasting here means checking a dish by putting a small amount in the mouth, which according to the standard explanation is then spat out. It does not mean eating a small portion of food.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לֵיהּ: טוֹעֵם וְאֵין בְּכָךְ כְּלוּם.
phrases.english: He said to him: He tastes, and it is of no concern.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לֵיהּ: טוֹעֵם וְאֵין בְּכָךְ כְּלוּם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אשיאן's question from Step 8
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A fasting person may taste food. Tasting does not break the fast.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports רבי אמי's answer
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that tasting food does not need a ברכה, and that a fasting person may taste without a problem. This matches רבי אמי's answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was also taught this way in a ברייתא: Tasting does not require a ברכה, and one who is fasting may taste and it is of no concern.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that says the same thing as רבי אמי, which supports his answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא states the answer word for word: a fasting person may taste. Its first line, that tasting needs no ברכה, shows the same idea from another side. Tasting is not counted as real eating, so it needs no ברכה and does not break a fast.

keyTerms.meaning: It was also taught this way in a ברייתא. Brings support
Tasting, checking a dish by tasting it
Requires a blessing

steps.whatToRemember: A person who is fasting may taste food to check it, and tasting does not require a ברכה. Both rules come from the same idea: tasting is not considered eating.
steps.whyThisMatters: This becomes practical הלכה about tasting food while cooking on a private fast day, and about which kinds of tasting need a ברכה.

phrases.english: It was also taught so in a baraita:
Tasting does not require a blessing,
phrases.notes: Because tasting is not considered eating.

phrases.english: and one who is fasting may taste
and it is of no concern.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רבי אמי's answer from Step 9 with a ברייתא
steps.raayaObject: רבי אמי's ruling that a fasting person may taste
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא: tasting requires no ברכה, and a fasting person may taste without concern

steps.title: How much may a fasting person taste?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the limit on tasting during a fast.
steps.simpleTranslation: Up to how much may he taste?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא has just learned that a fasting person may taste food. Now it asks a follow-up question: how much counts as "tasting"?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 9 and 10 allowed tasting, but they did not give an amount. Without a limit, "tasting" could turn into real eating. This question asks for that limit.

keyTerms.meaning: Up to how much? (asking for a measurement)

phrases.english: Up to how much?
phrases.notes: A short follow-up question about the tasting permitted in Step 9.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows up on the permission to taste by asking for its limit.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The maximum amount a fasting person may taste without it counting as breaking the fast.

steps.title: Tasting up to a רביעית
steps.stepSummary: רבי אמי and רבי אסי would taste up to a רביעית.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אמי and רבי אסי would taste up to the amount of a רביעית (a quarter of a לוג).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from what two great אמוראים actually did. When they fasted, they would taste up to a רביעית.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer comes from a real practice, not from a stated rule. It sets the limit at a רביעית, so anything up to that amount still counts as "tasting" and does not break the fast. The answer fits well because רבי אמי is the same חכם who allowed tasting in Step 9.

keyTerms.meaning: They would taste
A set halachic measurement
A quarter of a לוג, a common liquid measurement

steps.whatToRemember: A fasting person may taste food without a ברכה and without breaking the fast, up to a רביעית, as רבי אמי and רבי אסי did.
steps.confusionAlert: Tasting means testing the flavor of a dish, for example while cooking it. The גמרא itself does not say whether one must spit it out. The common practice, codified in שולחן ערוך, is to spit it out, so this is not permission to swallow a רביעית of food on a fast.

phrases.english: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi
would taste up to the measure of a quarter-log.
phrases.notes: This describes what they did when they were fasting.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the question of Step 11.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The limit is a רביעית, based on the practice of רבי אמי and רבי אסי.

steps.title: Greeting someone before praying
steps.stepSummary: רב rules that greeting a friend before תפלה is like building a במה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: Anyone who greets his friend before he prays is as if he built a במה (an altar for idol worship).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new topic with a strong statement from רב. Greeting another person before saying the morning תפלה is compared to building an altar for idol worship.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea is that a person's first attention in the morning belongs to God. Honoring a human being first gives that person a kind of honor that belongs to God alone, so רב compares it to building a במה. The topic connects to the earlier discussion of greeting people during קריאת שמע and הלל.

keyTerms.meaning: One who gives a greeting
Before he prays (the morning תפלה)
An altar, here meaning one used for idol worship
As if (a comparison, not a literal act)

steps.confusionAlert: רב does not mean the person actually worshipped idols. כְּאִילּוּ ("as if") is a strong comparison that shows how serious it is to put a person before God.

phrases.english: Rav said:
Anyone who gives a greeting to his fellow
before he prays,
it is as if he made him an altar.
phrases.notes: In other words, as if he treated the person like an object of worship.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב: כָּל הַנּוֹתֵן שָׁלוֹם לַחֲבֵירוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new topic, connected by theme to the earlier discussion of greetings.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Greeting a friend before the morning תפלה is as serious as building a במה.

steps.title: רב's source from a פסוק in ישעיה
steps.stepSummary: רב brings a פסוק from ישעיה and reads בַּמֶּה as בָּמָה.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it says: "Stop relying on man, whose breath is in his nostrils, for בַּמֶּה (how much) is he worth?" Do not read it as בַּמֶּה ("how much"); read it as בָּמָה ("altar").
steps.whatsHappening: רב proves his rule from a פסוק. He uses an אל תקרי reading, changing the vowels of one word so that בַּמֶּה ("how much") becomes בָּמָה ("altar").
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says to stay away from a person "whose breath is in his nostrils," which hints at the morning, when a person's breath and soul return to him. Reading the word as "altar" teaches that turning to a person first in the morning is like making him an altar. This gives רב's comparison a basis in the פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is said (introduces a פסוק as a source)
Stop / hold back
Breath in his nostrils
Do not read it as ..., but rather as ... (a drasha that changes the vowels of a word)

phrases.english: As it is said: "Cease from man,
phrases.notes: ישעיה 2:22

phrases.english: in whose nostrils is breath,
phrases.notes: Hints at the morning, when breath and the soul return.

phrases.english: for how much is he accounted?"
Do not read it as "bameh" (how much),
but rather as "bamah" (altar).
phrases.notes: Only the vowels change; the letters stay the same.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the פסוק behind רב's statement in Step 13.
steps.raayaObject: רב's rule that greeting someone before תפלה is like building a במה.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ישעיה 2:22, with בַּמֶּה read as בָּמָה.

steps.title: שמואל's plain reading of the פסוק
steps.stepSummary: שמואל reads בַּמֶּה literally: why did you consider this person important, and not God?
steps.simpleTranslation: And שמואל said: "In what way" did you consider this person important, and not God?
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל explains the same פסוק differently. He keeps the word בַּמֶּה with its plain meaning, "how much" or "in what way," and does not change it to "altar."
steps.deeperAnalysis: For שמואל, the פסוק is asking a sharp question: why did you think this person was worth honoring before God? He reaches the same practical message as רב, that God comes first in the morning. But he does not use the comparison to idol worship.

keyTerms.meaning: You considered him (important)
To God

steps.whatToRemember: Both רב and שמואל learn from ישעיה 2:22 that a person should not greet others before the morning תפלה. רב reads the word as בָּמָה (like idol worship). שמואל keeps the plain meaning: why would you honor a person before God?

phrases.english: And Shmuel said:
In what way did you consider this one (important)
and not God?
phrases.notes: Meaning: you should have honored God first.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different reading of the same פסוק that רב used in Step 14.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The פסוק criticizes honoring a person before God, read without the אל תקרי change.

steps.title: Challenge from the משנה: greeting is allowed between the paragraphs of קריאת שמע
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת challenges רב from our משנה, which allows greeting someone out of respect during the breaks of קריאת שמע. Since קריאת שמע comes before תפלה, greeting before תפלה seems to be allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת raised an objection: In the breaks between the paragraphs, a person may greet someone out of respect, and may answer a greeting!
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת attacks רב's rule (Step 13) by quoting our own משנה, which allows greeting during קריאת שמע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה lets you greet a respected person in the breaks between the paragraphs of קריאת שמע. קריאת שמע is said before the morning תפלה, so this is a greeting before תפלה. If greeting before תפלה were as bad as building a במה, how could the משנה allow it in the middle of מצוות like קריאת שמע?

keyTerms.meaning: Raises an objection, usually from a משנה or ברייתא
In the breaks between the paragraphs of קריאת שמע and its ברכות
Out of respect for an important person
Greets first, and answers a greeting

steps.confusionAlert: רב ששת is not quoting a new source. This is the משנה from earlier in this פרק (13a), used here as a weapon against רב.

phrases.english: Rav Sheshet raised an objection:
In the breaks between paragraphs, one may greet out of respect, and may answer a greeting!
phrases.notes: Quoted from the משנה (13a). Since קריאת שמע comes before תפלה, this looks like greeting before praying.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב's rule from Step 13 (backed up in Step 14) that greeting before תפלה is like building a במה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's ruling that greeting a friend before תפלה is forbidden, like building a במה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה allows greeting during the breaks of קריאת שמע, which is before תפלה. So greeting before תפלה cannot be totally forbidden.

steps.title: רבי אבא: the prohibition is only about going early to someone's door
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא narrows רב's rule. It only applies when a person goes early to someone's door just to greet him. A greeting by chance meeting is allowed, as in the משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא explained it: It refers to someone who goes early to the other person's door.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבא defends רב by limiting his rule to one specific case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב's prohibition is not about any greeting before תפלה. It is about going out of your way early in the morning, to someone's door, to honor him before you have honored ה׳. The משנה is talking about someone you just happen to meet, so there is no contradiction.

keyTerms.meaning: He explained it, meaning he gave a reading that solves the problem
Gets up early, goes out early
To his door

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the practical limit on רב's rule: the problem is going out of your way to honor a person before honoring ה׳, not a passing hello.

phrases.english: Rabbi Abba explained it:
It refers to one who goes early to his door.
phrases.notes: In other words, he goes specially to greet him before praying. A chance meeting is fine.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב ששת's challenge in Step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case: רב's rule covers only a special early visit, not a chance meeting.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב forbade any greeting at all before תפלה, which would clash with the משנה.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב only forbade going early to someone's door to greet him. The משנה's greeting during קריאת שמע is a chance meeting, so it is allowed.

steps.title: רבי זירא: doing your own business before praying is like building a במה
steps.stepSummary: רבי יונה quotes רבי זירא: anyone who takes care of his own affairs before praying is as if he built a במה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יונה said in the name of רבי זירא: Anyone who does his own business before he prays, it is as if he built a במה.
steps.whatsHappening: A new teaching is brought. It widens the topic from greeting people to doing any personal business before תפלה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב was talking about honoring a person before ה׳‎. רבי זירא, as quoted here, talks about taking care of your own needs before ה׳. The same harsh comparison to a במה is used, which sets up the next question.

keyTerms.meaning: His own affairs, his personal business
Before he prays
As if he built a private altar, which is forbidden

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָה אָמַר רַבִּי זֵירָא:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yona said in the name of Rabbi Zeira:
Anyone who does his own affairs
before he prays —
it is as if he built a bamah (forbidden altar).
phrases.notes: The same strong comparison רב used for greeting (Step 13).

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָה אָמַר רַבִּי זֵירָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from greeting people (רב) to doing any personal business before תפלה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Doing personal business before תפלה is as bad as building a במה.

steps.title: Did you really say 'במה'?
steps.stepSummary: The listeners ask רבי יונה whether he really said 'במה'.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: Did you say 'במה'?
steps.whatsHappening: The listeners check whether רבי יונה's wording was exact. This sets up his answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Comparing ordinary business to building a forbidden altar is a very harsh statement. So they ask if they heard the word correctly, or if רבי יונה really meant something that strong.

keyTerms.meaning: They said to him
Did you say? (Aramaic)

phrases.english: They said to him:
Did you say 'bamah'?
phrases.notes: They are checking the exact word he used.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the exact wording of רבי זירא's teaching from Step 18.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether רבי יונה really used the harsh word 'במה'.

steps.title: רבי יונה: I only said it is forbidden
steps.stepSummary: רבי יונה answers that he did not say 'במה'. He only said that it is 'אסור', forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: No, I was saying 'אסור' (it is forbidden).
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יונה corrects the wording. The rule is a plain prohibition, without the במה comparison.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule itself stays: you may not do your own business before praying. What drops is the extreme comparison to building a במה. So for personal business, the strength of the statement is toned down.

keyTerms.meaning: Forbidden
I am saying, I meant (Aramaic)

steps.confusionAlert: רבי יונה is not taking back the rule. Doing business before תפלה is still forbidden. He is only taking away the 'במה' comparison.

phrases.english: He said to them: No,
I was saying 'forbidden'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 19.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He said 'אסור', not 'במה'. Doing business before תפלה is forbidden, but it is not compared to building a במה.

steps.title: Support: רב יצחק בר אשיאן forbids personal business before prayer, from a פסוק
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא backs up רבי יונה's version with רב יצחק בר אשיאן's teaching. A person may not do his own business before praying, based on the פסוק 'צדק לפניו יהלך'.
steps.simpleTranslation: This matches what רב אידי בר אבין said in the name of רב יצחק בר אשיאן: A person may not do his own business before he prays, as it says: 'Righteousness shall go before Him, and then He will set His steps on the way.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that the plain word 'אסור' fits another known teaching, which also gives a source from תהלים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יצחק בר אשיאן uses the same word, 'אסור', with no mention of a במה, so this supports רבי יונה's correction. The פסוק teaches the order: first 'צדק', meaning praying and declaring ה׳'s righteousness. Only after that, 'set his steps on the way', meaning going about your own business.

keyTerms.meaning: And this fits with what Rav (so-and-so) said
As it is said (introduces a פסוק)
Righteousness shall go before Him (תהלים פה:יד): first pray
His steps, meaning going on his way and his business

steps.whatToRemember: Final picture: (1) Greeting before תפלה is like building a במה only when you go early to someone's door on purpose. A chance greeting is fine. (2) Doing your own business before תפלה is forbidden (אסור), but not compared to a במה. The source is 'צדק לפניו יהלך': first ה׳, then your own path.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for the practical הלכה that one should not start personal work or errands in the morning before davening.

phrases.english: (And this fits what Rav Idi bar Avin said,)
phrases.notes: Links רבי יונה's corrected wording to a known teaching.

phrases.aramaic: רַב אִידִי בַּר אָבִין אָמַר רַב יִצְחָק בַּר אַשְׁיָאן:
phrases.english: Rav Idi bar Avin said in the name of Rav Yitzchak bar Ashyan:
It is forbidden for a person to do his own affairs
before he prays, as it is said:
'Righteousness shall go before Him,'
phrases.notes: First pray and declare ה׳'s righteousness.

phrases.english: 'and then he will set his steps on the way.'
phrases.notes: Only afterward go out on your own path and business. (תהלים פה:יד)

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רבי יונה's corrected wording from Step 20 ('אסור', not 'במה') with a parallel teaching and a פסוק.
steps.raayaObject: That doing personal business before תפלה is forbidden, stated as 'אסור' without the במה comparison.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב יצחק בר אשיאן (through רב אידי בר אבין), based on תהלים פה:יד: 'צדק לפניו יהלך וישם לדרך פעמיו'.

steps.title: Pray first, then travel, and ה׳ takes care of your needs
steps.stepSummary: רב אידי בר אבין quotes רב יצחק בר אשיאן: whoever prays and only then sets out on the road, הקדוש ברוך הוא takes care of his needs. The source is the same פסוק, 'צדק לפניו יהלך'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אידי בר אבין said in the name of רב יצחק בר אשיאן: Anyone who prays first and only then leaves for a journey, הקדוש ברוך הוא takes care of his needs, as the פסוק says: 'Righteousness (prayer) will walk before him, and He will set his footsteps on the path.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second teaching from רב יצחק בר אשיאן. This time it shows the reward for praying before going about your day.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 21 used 'צדק לפניו יהלך' to forbid doing your own business before praying. Here the same פסוק promises a reward: if prayer goes first, ה׳ 'sets your footsteps on the path' and takes care of your needs. The prohibition and the reward come from the same verse.

keyTerms.meaning: Sets out on a journey
Takes care of his needs and wishes
And He will set his footsteps on the path

steps.whyThisMatters: Together with Step 21, this gives the full picture. Praying before your own affairs is required, and it also brings a blessing. It is the basis for the practice of davening before leaving on a trip.

phrases.english: And Rav Idi bar Avin said
phrases.notes: Attribution line, merged into the teaching it introduces.

phrases.english: Rav Yitzchak bar Ashyan said:
phrases.notes: The same אמורא whose teaching was quoted in Step 21.

phrases.english: Anyone who prays and afterward
sets out on the road,

phrases.aramaic: הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא עוֹשֶׂה לוֹ חֲפָצָיו,
phrases.english: the Holy One, Blessed be He, takes care of his needs,
as it says: 'Righteousness will walk before him,'
phrases.notes: 'צדק' is read as prayer, which goes first.

phrases.english: 'and He will set his footsteps on the path.'
phrases.notes: The second half of the פסוק is the source of the reward.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַב אִידִי בַּר אָבִין אָמַר רַב יִצְחָק בַּר אַשְׁיָאן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second teaching from the same Amora, using the same פסוק, showing the reward that goes with the rule in Step 21.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who prays before setting out on a journey merits that ה׳ takes care of his needs.

steps.title: Seven nights without a dream
steps.stepSummary: Because רבי יונה was mentioned earlier, the גמרא brings another teaching he said in the name of רבי זירא. Someone who sleeps seven nights without dreaming is called 'רע'. This is learned by reading 'שָׂבֵעַ' (satisfied) as 'שֶׁבַע' (seven).
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יונה said in the name of רבי זירא: Anyone who sleeps seven nights without a dream is called 'evil', as the פסוק says: 'He will sleep satisfied, he will not be visited, evil.' Do not read 'שׂבע' (satisfied). Read it as 'שבע' (seven).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a side topic. It brings another teaching from רבי יונה, who was mentioned in Steps 18-20, and this one is about dreams.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new reading takes the פסוק as: 'one who sleeps seven nights and is not visited by a dream is called רע'. The idea is that if ה׳ sends him no dream at all, it suggests he is distant from ה׳. This is a word-play reading, an 'אל תקרי', and it changes only the vowels.

keyTerms.meaning: One who sleeps or stays overnight
Dream
He will not be visited (remembered)
Do not read it as... (a word-play reading of a פסוק)

steps.confusionAlert: 'אל תקרי' does not mean the text of the פסוק is wrong. It is a teaching method that reads the same letters with different vowels to draw out an extra lesson.

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָה אָמַר רַבִּי זֵירָא:
phrases.english: And Rabbi Yona said in the name of Rabbi Zeira:
phrases.notes: The same chain of transmission as in Step 18.

phrases.english: Anyone who sleeps seven nights (days)
without a dream is called 'evil',
as it says: 'He will sleep satisfied,'
phrases.notes: משלי 19:23

phrases.english: 'he will not be visited, evil',
phrases.notes: Read here as: one who is not 'visited' by a dream is 'רע'.

phrases.english: Do not read 'save'a' (satisfied)
but rather 'sheva' (seven).

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָה אָמַר רַבִּי זֵירָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A side teaching brought because רבי יונה's name came up earlier; it is not related to the topic of prayer.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who goes seven nights without a dream is called 'רע'.

steps.title: A different reading: one who goes to sleep full of Torah hears no bad news
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא, the son of רבי חייא בר אבא, says that the real tradition from רבי יוחנן reads the פסוק differently. Whoever fills himself with Torah and then goes to sleep will not be told bad news.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא, son of רבי חייא בר אבא, said to him: This is what רבי חייא said in the name of רבי יוחנן: Anyone who fills himself with words of Torah and goes to sleep, they do not bring him bad news, as it says: 'He will sleep satisfied, he will not be visited by evil.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא pushes back on רבי יונה's reading. He says the correct tradition reads the same פסוק simply, without any 'אל תקרי'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יונה changed 'satisfied' into 'seven'. רב אחא keeps 'satisfied' and explains it as satisfied with Torah, while 'בל יפקד רע' now means no bad news will reach him. With 'הכי אמר' ('this is how it was taught'), he sets a different tradition on this פסוק, from רבי יוחנן, against רבי יונה's negative reading. That sets aside the dream teaching.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what he said (introducing a corrected version of a tradition)
One who fills (satisfies) himself
Bad news

steps.whatToRemember: The same פסוק, 'ושבע ילין בל יפקד רע', is read in two ways. רבי יונה reads it as seven nights without a dream, which is called רע. רב אחא, quoting רבי יוחנן, reads it as going to sleep full of Torah, which protects you from bad news.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא:
phrases.english: Rav Acha, son of Rabbi Chiya bar Abba, said to him:

phrases.aramaic: הָכִי אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: This is what Rabbi Chiya said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan:
phrases.notes: 'הכי' introduces a different tradition on the same פסוק, set against רבי יונה's reading.

phrases.aramaic: כָּל הַמַּשְׂבִּיעַ עַצְמוֹ מִדִּבְרֵי תּוֹרָה וְלָן —
phrases.english: Anyone who fills himself with words of Torah and goes to sleep —
they do not bring him bad news,
as it says: 'He will sleep satisfied,'
phrases.notes: Here 'satisfied' keeps its plain meaning: satisfied with Torah.

phrases.english: 'he will not be visited by evil.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא הָכִי אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a competing tradition that reads the same פסוק differently, setting aside רבי יונה's dream reading.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the 'אל תקרי' reading of the פסוק as being about seven nights without a dream.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: A competing tradition from רבי יוחנן reads 'ושבע' plainly as 'satisfied with Torah', a praise, rather than reading it as 'seven' in a negative way.

steps.title: Quoting the next line of the משנה: the breaks between the paragraphs
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the משנה and quotes its next phrase, 'אלו הן בין הפרקים', to begin discussing it.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned in the משנה: 'These are the breaks between the paragraphs,' and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a new discussion. It quotes the next words of the משנה, about the breaks between the paragraphs of קריאת שמע, so that it can analyze them next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This line does not teach anything new by itself. It is a heading that opens the next topic. The משנה lists the points between the paragraphs and ברכות of שמע where interrupting is more permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: Between the paragraphs (the breaks in קריאת שמע and its brachos)
Etc. (the rest of the quote is understood)

phrases.english: These are the breaks between the paragraphs, etc.
phrases.notes: A quote from the משנה that opens the next discussion.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the side teachings and returns to the משנה to open a new topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Introduces the משנה's list of the breaks between the paragraphs of קריאת שמע.

steps.title: The law follows רבי יהודה: no stopping between אלהיכם and אמת ויציב
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו quotes רבי יוחנן: the הלכה follows רבי יהודה, who rules that one may not interrupt between 'אלהיכם' and 'אמת ויציב'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבהו said in the name of רבי יוחנן: The law is like רבי יהודה, who said that a person may not stop between 'אלהיכם' and 'אמת ויציב'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the final practical ruling on רבי יהודה's view from the משנה. You may not pause between the end of קריאת שמע and the next ברכה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה had a general list of 'בין הפרקים', the breaks between sections where some interruption is allowed. רבי יהודה made one exception: the gap between the end of the third פרשה and 'אמת ויציב' does not count as a break. רבי יוחנן rules that we follow רבי יהודה, so this spot is treated as one continuous unit.

keyTerms.meaning: The law follows (this opinion)
He may not interrupt or pause
'Your God', the last word of קריאת שמע ('אני ה׳ אלהיכם')
'True and firm', the opening words of the ברכה after קריאת שמע

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think 'בין הפרקים' means you may always stop between any two sections. רבי יהודה's rule, which is the הלכה, makes the gap between 'אלהיכם' and 'אמת ויציב' an exception where you may not stop.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a practical ruling for how we say קריאת שמע every day. We go straight from 'אלהיכם' into 'אמת' with no pause.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Abbahu said that Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
The law is in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda
who said that between 'Eloheikhem' and 'Emet veyatziv'
phrases.notes: 'אלהיכם' ends the third פרשה; 'אמת ויציב' begins the ברכה after it.

phrases.english: one may not interrupt.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: הֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Step 25 quoted the משנה's phrase 'אלו הן בין הפרקים'. This step gives the binding ruling on רבי יהודה's exception within that list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The הלכה follows רבי יהודה. One may not interrupt between 'אלהיכם' and 'אמת ויציב'.

steps.title: What is רבי יהודה's reason? The גמרא begins to cite a פסוק
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו, again in רבי יוחנן's name, asks for the reason behind רבי יהודה's ruling and starts to answer with 'דכתיב'. The פסוק itself comes on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבהו said in the name of רבי יוחנן: What is רבי יהודה's reason? As it is written:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רבי יהודה says you cannot stop there. It is setting up the answer, a פסוק that is quoted right after this line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now that we know the הלכה follows רבי יהודה, the גמרא wants the source behind his rule. The word 'דכתיב' tells us the answer will come from a פסוק. That פסוק will show why 'אלהיכם' and 'אמת' belong together without a break.

keyTerms.meaning: What is his reason?

phrases.english: Rabbi Abbahu said that Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
What is the reason of Rabbi Yehuda?
As it is written:

steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source or reason for רבי יהודה's rule that one may not interrupt between 'אלהיכם' and 'אמת ויציב'.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The answer begins with 'דכתיב', a פסוק that is quoted on the next amud.
